editorNote: Color, sound and the promise of a new home-computer platform take center stage.
morningLine: Amiga arrives on stage; the home-computer future gets a vivid new palette.

milestone.title: Commodore unveils the Amiga
milestone.note: The July 23 introduction established a landmark multimedia personal-computer platform whose color graphics, sound and creative demonstrations helped define the next era of home computing.

lead.headline: Amiga takes the stage: Commodore bets on color and creativity
lead.dek: A $1,295 computer makes its New York debut, with September shipments promised.
body: Commodore unveiled its Amiga on July 23 at the Vivian Beaumont Theater in New York’s Lincoln Center. The Motorola 68000-based computer arrives with a striking brief: make color graphics, sound and creative work central to the personal-computer experience. The announced computer price is $1,295; that figure should not be confused with a monitor-inclusive package.

The stage demonstration gave that ambition a familiar face. Andy Warhol digitized and recolored a portrait of Blondie singer Debbie Harry with ProPaint, a paint system still being tested. Rather than presenting the computer only as an office appliance, Commodore put image-making before the audience.

The entertainment industry is watching, too. Electronic Arts founder Trip Hawkins has championed the machine’s home-entertainment potential. For game makers, an ambitious new platform offers another direction beyond the established 8-bit machines, although a demonstration is not a shelf full of finished games.

Commodore acquired Amiga in August 1984 and is now positioning the machine against Apple’s Macintosh. The company says shipments will begin in September. This week marks the unveiling, not verified retail availability: buyers must still wait to see the promised machine reach dealers.

stories.headline: Kennedy Approach puts talking aircraft on the home-computer radar
body: MicroProse is promoting Kennedy Approach for Commodore 64 and Atari computers in July’s Antic. The $34.95 suggested-retail simulation asks the player to manage aircraft around busy airports, bringing them in and sending them out while keeping traffic safely separated.

The advertisement makes speech part of the attraction, crediting Electronic Speech Systems of Berkeley, California. Multiple aircraft and emergencies supply the pressure. The printed screenshot is labeled Commodore-64; it is not evidence of how the Atari edition looks.

This is a publisher’s advertisement, not an independent flight test or proof of a particular July release day. Still, it captures an appealing change in home-computer play: the drama comes from directing a complicated system rather than firing at it.

stories.headline: Atari 130XE keeps 8-bit compatibility while doubling memory
body: While 16-bit machines compete for attention, Atari’s 130XE offers a different path: more room for an established 8-bit family. Jack Powell’s July Antic technical report describes 128K of RAM, with the extra 64K reached through bank switching.

A 16K window exposes the extended memory, and both the processor and ANTIC display chip can use it in different combinations. Atari says software that does not use the extra memory will be compatible with the 64K 65XE, which in turn is billed as compatible with the 800XL.

The Enhanced Cartridge Interface extends the cartridge slot, but Powell leaves physical compatibility with existing XL peripheral-bus equipment unresolved. These are July specifications, not a fresh announcement pinned to this week: prospective owners should keep the distinction between documented design and accessory promises in mind.

stories.headline: One disk, three jobs: HomePak courts the home office
body: Batteries Included is advertising HomePak at $49.95 in July’s Antic, offering three everyday applications on one diskette. HomeText handles word processing, HomeFind information management, and HomeTerm telecommunications.

The pitch is convenience: simple-English commands and on-screen menus for the newcomer, with additional commands for experienced users. Combining writing, filing and communications gives a home computer more to do between game sessions.

The advertisement cites a 1984 readers’ choice award and reproduces selected praise. This is an existing package receiving July promotion, not a newly established launch, and advertiser-selected reviews are no substitute for trying the software.

briefs.headline: Spinnaker responds to Atari owners
briefs.summary: In a July Antic letter, chairman William Bowman says the company is talking with Atari about products for the new machines; he explains platform decisions in terms of market growth, audience and development costs. Do not turn discussions into announced software commitments.

market.headline: A new platform must turn demonstrations into a software shelf
market.summary: The Amiga unveiling puts creative computing and entertainment in the spotlight. September shipping is a company plan, while Atari owners can already study July promotions for familiar-machine software and modems.

worldAnchor.headline: Rock Hudson’s spokesman confirms AIDS diagnosis
worldAnchor.summary: On July 25 in Paris, spokesman Yanou Collart confirmed that actor Rock Hudson had AIDS, according to an Associated Press dispatch. The announcement brought the illness into a new national spotlight.

bbsNote.headline: A $79.95 modem and a magazine that keeps updating online
bbsNote.summary: July Antic ties low-cost Atari communications hardware to CompuServe, Dow Jones information access and an online editorial service. These are documented July offers and publication notes, not July 22–28 launch claims.

posts.text: ADD-ON Systems advertises the Atari 1030 modem/software package for $79.95. The ad specifies at least 16K and a telephone line; disk communication software is included for disk-drive owners. Introductory subscriptions to CompuServe and Dow Jones Retrieval Services are included.

July Help! says ANTIC ONLINE carries current Atari news, including ST developments, with no surcharge beyond standard CompuServe hourly fees. Affiliated Worldwide Users Network groups can download special bulletins for newsletter reprinting.

The July column previews August material on Russ Wetmore and the 1030, a terminal program, and a program for animated cartoons on BBSs. These are previews, not claims that the August articles were already published.

curiosity.headline: A miniature-golf game that lets you redesign the course
curiosity.summary: July Antic gives readers a construction set alongside its type-in Miniature Golf game.
curiosity.detail: David Plotkin’s construction program generates data statements to append to the game. The article recommends graph paper and lays out a Graphics 7 design grid of 160 by 80 positions with seven prefabricated obstacle types. The game even allows a START-button do-over that does not add to the score—if opponents agree.
